summary: At two people per square mile, Inyo County is one of the least densely populated places in the contiguous United States — yet it contains both the highest point in the Lower 48 (Mount Whitney, 14,505 feet) and the lowest (Badwater Basin in Death Valley, 282 feet below sea level), a vertical spread of nearly three miles within a single county boundary. That geological drama defines daily life: the county seat of Bishop sits at about 4,150 feet on the Owens Valley floor, flanked by the Sierra Nevada to the west and the White-Inyo Mountains to the east, delivering panoramic alpenglow sunsets that are less a perk than a permanent backdrop. Employment centers around federal land management, the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (which has controlled much of the valley's water since the early twentieth century), tourism, and a modest healthcare and retail sector — job switching without relocating means a thin labor market. A median home value of $338,400 against a median household income of $72,432 yields a price-to-income ratio around 4.7, manageable compared to coastal California but paired with median rents of $1,140 that reflect limited housing stock rather than urban amenity. With 10.2 hours of daily sunshine on average, winters are cold and bright at elevation, summers searingly hot in the eastern desert lowlands. The tradeoff is elemental: unmatched access to wilderness and open sky, measured against geographic isolation and an economy built more around the land itself than any single private industry.
